Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

know verb

a person or place

also be acquainted with, get to know

classical

Plaut. As. 464
Traupman 17

nōvī, nōvisse

verb: perfect of nōscō with present sense (nōstī, nōram, nōsse)

know (a person, a place, something one is familiar with)

Properly “I have got to know”, so “I know”; nōveram or nōram is “I knew”. Latin keeps sciō for facts and nōvī for acquaintance: ut vīlicus nātūram agrī nōvit, dispēnsātor litterās scit (Cic. Rep. 5.3.5, cited by Lewis & Short, s.v. sciō).

Examples

  • nam mellītus erat suamque nōrat ipsam tam bene quam puella mātrem

    for he was sweet as honey, and knew his mistress as well as a little girl knows her motherCatull. 3.6–7

  • ego, ille quem nōstī, aprōs trēs et quidem pulcherrimōs cēpī

    I, yes, the man you know, have caught three boars, and fine ones tooPlin. Ep. 1.6.1

  • Ulixēs, quem nōstī, vir ille cui Aeolus ventōs in utre clausōs dedit

    Ulysses, whom you know, the man Aeolus gave the winds to, shut up in a bagLibellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae

Other words

  • cognōscō, cognōscere, cognōvī, cognitum — get to know, learn; in the perfect, know

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Phaedr. 3.4.7: multōs cognōvī optimōs

    Lewis & Short: in the perfect tenses “to know”, very frequent in every period.

  • nōscō, nōscere, nōvī, nōtum — get to know (in the present tenses)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Traupman 102

    The present means “get to know”: told “I don’t know him”, a character in Plautus answers at nōsce sānē, “well, get to know him, then” (Plaut. As. 464).

See also know, friend.

SourcesLewis & Short: nosco · Lewis & Short: cognosco · Lewis & Short: scio
